units.title: Unit 41 — Youth and age
learningObjectives: Use age-related collocations accurately for early childhood, adolescence and family relationships.
Describe routines, relationships and life changes during adulthood with natural verbs and noun phrases.
Discuss ageing, personal memories and attention with sensitivity to idiomatic register.
Explain meaning contrasts such as leave home versus leave the house and fall into versus fit into a pattern.

items.example: The nurses showed the parents how to hold their newborn baby safely.
items.note: Newborn normally modifies baby to emphasise the earliest stage after birth.

items.example: Her adoring parents applauded even the smallest progress she made.
items.note: Adoring conveys exceptionally affectionate admiration, not simply responsible parenting.

items.example: The child prodigy composed a short piano piece before turning eight.
items.note: Prodigy refers to a child with an exceptional talent, especially in a demanding field.

items.pt: satisfazer todos os caprichos de alguém
items.example: His grandparents pander to his every whim, even when his requests are unreasonable.
items.note: Pander to carries disapproval and suggests indulging someone instead of setting limits.

items.example: The boy acted like a spoilt brat when the game did not go his way.
items.note: This strongly disapproving, informal expression describes badly behaved children; spoilt is British English.

items.example: As a young teenager, Maya preferred drawing to going to parties.
items.note: Young teenager normally refers to someone in the early teenage years.

items.example: He started to hang around with older students after school.
items.note: Hang around with is informal and focuses on spending time with a particular group.

items.example: The programme created apprenticeships for disaffected youth in the city.
items.note: Disaffected signals alienation or dissatisfaction with established institutions or social expectations.

items.example: The neighbourhood was on the verge of losing its only youth centre.
items.note: On the verge of is followed by a noun or an -ing form and suggests an imminent development.

items.example: The mentor helped a former juvenile delinquent return to school.
items.note: Juvenile delinquent is a legal or institutional label for a young offender; avoid casually labelling children.

items.example: She has a talent for calming anxious children.
items.note: Have a talent for takes a noun or gerund and describes a natural ability.

items.word: see the error of one's ways
items.example: After hearing the victims, he finally saw the error of his ways.
items.note: This idiom implies recognising and often changing past wrong behaviour.

items.example: She spent her teenage years in a small coastal town.
items.note: Teenage years is a conventional plural noun phrase for the period from thirteen to nineteen.

items.example: Local radio stations helped shape youth culture in the region.
items.note: Youth culture refers to shared styles, tastes and practices among young people.

items.example: The volunteers made a considerable contribution to the restoration project.
items.note: Make a contribution to is the conventional verb-preposition pattern; considerable marks substantial importance.

items.example: Both of her grandparents married young and raised large families.
items.note: Marry young describes the age at marriage; do not insert at before young.

items.example: The couple had a baby shortly after moving to the village.
items.note: Have a baby is idiomatic for giving birth or becoming parents; get a baby is not the normal choice.

items.pt: cair ou entrar em um padrão
items.example: Without planning it, the team fell into a pattern of late-night meetings.
items.note: Fall into suggests that a repeated routine develops gradually, often without conscious choice.

items.example: Remote work made it easier for him to balance family life and study.
items.note: Family life refers collectively to domestic roles and relationships.

items.example: The school aims to provide a stable environment for every pupil.
items.note: Stable combines naturally with environment to mean secure, consistent conditions.

items.example: They neglected their relationship while concentrating entirely on their careers.
items.note: Neglect describes insufficient care or attention, not necessarily an intentional rejection.

items.pt: não dar o devido valor a alguém
items.example: She realised she had taken her closest friends for granted.
items.note: The fixed expression means failing to appreciate someone because their presence seems assured.

items.pt: sair da casa dos pais para morar fora
items.example: He left home at nineteen to study in another city.
items.note: Leave home usually implies moving away from the family household, rather than stepping outside briefly.

items.pt: ir estudar na universidade, geralmente em outra cidade
items.example: In September, their youngest daughter went off to university.
items.note: Go off to highlights departure for a new stage or destination.

items.pt: passar por uma crise de meia-idade
items.example: He went through a midlife crisis and questioned his long-term plans.
items.note: Go through a crisis is the idiomatic pattern; the crisis is experienced, not gone against.

items.example: Changing her daily routine helped her sleep more regularly.
items.note: Daily routine is the established combination for habitual everyday activities.

items.example: The child is going through a phase of refusing unfamiliar foods.
items.note: A phase is understood as temporary; go through is the natural verb pairing.

items.example: We had no choice but to postpone the trip after the storm.
items.note: This structure is followed by the base verb and expresses a lack of viable alternatives.

items.example: The staff respected her wishes and kept the discussion private.
items.note: Respect wishes means honour what a person wants; admire wishes does not convey this meaning.

items.word: set off on a road trip
items.pt: partir para uma viagem de carro
items.example: They set off on a road trip along the northern coast.
items.note: Set off marks the start of a journey; on introduces the road trip.

items.example: After climbing six flights of stairs, he began to feel his age.
items.note: Feel your age means become conscious of physical limitations associated with ageing.

items.example: An occasional twinge in her shoulder reminded her to take breaks.
items.note: Twinge is a brief, mild pain; occasional stresses that it occurs infrequently.

items.pt: lapso de memória atribuído à idade
items.example: I forgot the access code again and joked that I was having a senior moment.
items.note: This is informal and potentially age-stereotyping; use sparingly and avoid in respectful clinical contexts.

items.example: He called himself a grumpy old man whenever the neighbours played loud music.
items.note: Grumpy old man is an informal, often disparaging stereotype of an older man who complains.

items.example: After retirement, they were able to lead a comfortable life near their family.
items.note: Lead a life and live a life are natural combinations; comfortable indicates material ease or security.

items.example: I have only a hazy memory of the apartment where I lived as a child.
items.note: Hazy describes a memory whose details are unclear, unlike a distinct memory.

items.example: The cracked bowl had sentimental value because it belonged to her grandmother.
items.note: Sentimental value concerns emotional significance, not an item's selling price.

items.example: Reading for fifteen minutes before bed soon became a habit.
items.note: A behaviour becomes a habit, whereas a person develops a habit.

items.pt: examinar álbuns de fotos com atenção
items.example: On rainy afternoons, they pored over photo albums from their travels.
items.note: Pore over means study with close attention; the verb is pore, not pour.

items.example: The old school song rekindled memories of her first friends.
items.note: Rekindle figuratively means bring memories or feelings back to life.

items.example: They enjoyed telling stories about the slower pace of days gone by.
items.note: Days gone by is a nostalgic set phrase for the past.

items.pt: dar toda a atenção a alguém
items.example: During the conversation, the counsellor gave the child her undivided attention.
items.note: Undivided attention means full concentration without competing distractions.

items.word: not let someone out of your sight
items.pt: não tirar os olhos de alguém
items.example: At the busy festival, she would not let her little brother out of her sight.
items.note: The fixed phrase means keeping someone continuously within view, often for safety.

items.example: We checked that no one had come to harm during the evacuation.
items.note: Come to harm is often used in negative statements and concerns injury or misfortune.

items.pt: sair de casa por um momento
items.example: I left the house to buy bread and returned ten minutes later.
items.note: Unlike leave home, leave the house normally just means physically going outdoors.

items.example: She has a distinct memory of seeing snow for the first time.
items.note: Distinct contrasts with hazy and signals a clear, well-defined recollection.

items.example: A sudden twinge in his ankle made him stop walking.
items.note: Sudden describes the unexpected onset of a brief pain; occasional describes frequency.

items.example: He developed a habit of checking his phone before breakfast.
items.note: A person develops a habit, but a behaviour becomes a habit.

items.example: The new observations fit into a pattern the researchers had already identified.
items.note: Fit into refers to matching an established pattern; fall into suggests developing one.

items.example: Although she looks her age, she remains extremely energetic.
items.note: Look your age describes appearance, while feel your age describes subjective experience.

items.example: The familiar scent stirred up memories of childhood holidays.
items.note: Stir up memories emphasises provoking recollections, sometimes strongly emotional.

items.example: The siblings met regularly to share memories of their hometown.
items.note: Share memories means recounting recollections with others; it does not mean recalling them privately.

units.title: Unit 42 — Celebrities and heroes
learningObjectives: Use media collocations to describe celebrity interviews, publicity, personal accounts and luxury lifestyles.
Report honours, career achievements and critical reception using natural awards vocabulary.
Distinguish strong and conventional verb-noun combinations for praise, impact and success.
Recognise subtle distinctions between exclusive and in-depth interviews, nominations and winning awards.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: The actor gave an exclusive interview to a small independent newspaper.
items.note: Exclusive signals that an outlet obtained an interview unavailable to rival outlets.

items.word: let someone in on a secret
items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: She let her sister in on a secret about the surprise party.
items.note: The informal phrasal construction means disclose something not widely known.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: The couple had a fairytale wedding in a restored country house.
items.note: Fairytale suggests a romantic, idealised celebration, often with elaborate arrangements.

items.pt: levar um estilo de vida luxuoso
items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: The influencer appeared to lead a lavish lifestyle despite uncertain earnings.
items.note: Lavish describes extravagant spending or luxury; lead a lifestyle is a natural verbal pairing.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: Sources close to the singer confirmed that the tour had been postponed.
items.note: Journalistic sources close to someone may be colleagues, friends or associates, not only relatives.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: The documentary promised to reveal the truth behind the dispute.
items.note: Reveal naturally takes truth when concealed facts are being disclosed.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: Their lawyers drafted a prenuptial agreement before the ceremony.
items.note: Prenuptial means before marriage and commonly modifies agreement in legal contexts.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: A former athlete refused to sell her story to a tabloid.
items.note: Sell your story refers to receiving payment for a personal account, especially in the media.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: The rare manuscript was sold to the highest bidder at auction.
items.note: The highest bidder offers the most money; highest does not describe social status.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: The journalist conducted an in-depth interview about the director's early career.
items.note: In-depth means detailed and probing, contrasting with a superficial interview.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: He declined to reveal a secret entrusted to him years earlier.
items.note: Reveal a secret is a conventional verb-noun pairing for disclosing private information.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: She found the full glare of publicity difficult to cope with after the trial.
items.note: This figurative phrase evokes intense public scrutiny, not literally bright light.

items.section: A · Contents of a celebrity magazine
items.example: The federation investigated allegations of match fixing in the lower leagues.
items.note: Match fixing refers to illegally arranging sporting outcomes, usually for unfair gain.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: The university held an event to celebrate its graduates' achievements.
items.note: Celebrate achievements focuses on recognising completed accomplishments.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: Her first full-length feature film premiered at a regional festival.
items.note: A feature film is a cinema-length work; full-length highlights that it is not a short film.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: The new exhibition was highly praised for its imaginative design.
items.note: Highly is a natural intensifier of praised; the pairing signals strong approval.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: The musician received a nomination for best newcomer.
items.note: Receive a nomination is standard awards vocabulary; nomination is not itself a win.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: The researcher received a prestigious award for public engagement.
items.note: Prestigious refers to an award's reputation or status, not its monetary value.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: The play earned rave reviews after its opening night.
items.note: Rave reviews are enthusiastic evaluations, often by critics, rather than merely adequate reviews.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: She finally realised her ambition of opening a community theatre.
items.note: Realise an ambition means achieve a long-held goal, not merely understand it.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: The singer's meteoric rise to fame surprised even her producers.
items.note: Meteoric describes exceptionally fast prominence and is more emphatic than a gradual rise.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: Reviewers heaped praise on the cast for their performances.
items.note: Heap praise on is a vivid idiom for abundant, emphatic approval.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: The choreographer developed a unique approach to teaching movement.
items.note: Unique approach highlights a distinctive method; approach to takes a noun or -ing form.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: The festival invited a former winner to present an award.
items.note: Present an award describes formally giving a prize to its recipient.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: For the conductor, the national prize was the highest accolade of her career.
items.note: Accolade denotes special recognition or praise; highest intensifies its rank.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: The filmmaker's work had a significant impact on local arts education.
items.note: Have a significant impact on is the natural pattern; strong impact is less idiomatic here.

items.section: B · Speech at an awards ceremony
items.example: Fellow writers paid glowing tributes to the novelist after her retirement.
items.note: Glowing tributes are strongly positive expressions of appreciation, often in public or journalism.

items.example: The debut album enjoyed great success across several countries.
items.note: Enjoy great success and have great success are idiomatic; make great success is not.

items.example: The educational programme had great success in rural communities.
items.note: Have great success describes a successful outcome; avoid make great success.

items.example: Despite early setbacks, they made a success of their new restaurant.
items.note: Make a success of takes a noun describing a project, role or venture.

items.example: The documentary received rave reviews at its first screening.
items.note: Receive rave reviews combines a standard reception verb with highly enthusiastic evaluations.

items.example: Her nomination for an award brought attention to her independent film.
items.note: Nomination for specifies the honour or category for which someone is considered.

items.example: The adaptation was highly praised by critics for its performances.
items.note: Passive be highly praised by critics is common in reviews and award reporting.

items.example: The charity made a significant impact on access to books in the town.
items.note: Make an impact on is another idiomatic verb pattern alongside have an impact on.
